It's a thin wrapper around the agent CLI that talks to the control plane first. #!/bin/bash # byok-agent - a wrapper for Claude Code, Codex, or any other agent set -euo pipefail CONTROL_PLANE_URL = "${CONTROL_PLANE_URL:-http://localhost:8080}" AGENT_ID = "${AGENT_ID:-claude-code}" MODEL = "${MODEL:-anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet}" USER_ID = "${USER_ID:-$(whoami)}" # Step 1: Request authorization AUTH_RESPONSE = $( curl -s -X POST "$CONTROL_PLANE_URL/authorize" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"agent_id\":\"$AGENT_ID\",\"model\":\"$MODEL\",\"tools\":[\"read_file\",\"write_file\"],\"user_id\":\"$USER_ID\",\"requested_tokens\":100000}" ) ALLOWED = $( echo "$AUTH_RESPONSE" | jq -r '.allowed' ) if [ "$ALLOWED" != "true" ] ; then echo "Authorization denied: $(echo " $AUTH_RESPONSE " | jq -r '.reason')" >& 2 exit 1 fi SESSION_ID = $( echo "$AUTH_RESPONSE" | jq -r '.session_id' ) KEY_REF = $( echo "$AUTH_RESPONSE" | jq -r '.key_ref' ) # Step 2: Launch the agent via the runtime plane curl -s -X POST "$CONTROL_PLANE_URL/launch" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"agent_id\":\"$AGENT_ID\",\"session_id\":\"$SESSION_ID\",\"key_ref\":\"$KEY_REF\"}" # Step 3: The agent runs with the key injected by the runtime plane # The runtime plane sets AGENT_API_KEY in the environment. This is the complete flow. The developer never sees the key. The policy engine never sees the key. The runtime plane fetches it from Vault only at the moment of execution. Deep Dive: Policy Enforcement and Secure Key Injection The previous tutorial showed a basic implementation. Now let's examine the security-critical aspects in more detail. Key Rotation and Versioning One of the biggest advantages of a control plane is that you can rotate keys without touching the developer's machine. When you rotate a key in Vault, you simply update the secret. The next time an agent runs, the runtime plane fetches the new version. There's no need to redistribute keys to hundreds of developers. But there's a subtlety: if an agent is already running, it holds the old key. The runtime plane should support graceful revocation . We can do this by having the runtime plane monitor a "key version" in Vault. If the version changes mid-run, the runtime plane can send a SIGTERM to the agent process, forcing it to restart with the new key. This is a simple but effective pattern. Session Tokens and Short-Lived Credentials Instead of passing the actual API key to the agent, you can pass a short-lived token that the agent exchanges for the real key at the provider's side. This is what AWS STS does for IAM roles. For Claude and Codex, this is harder because they expect a static API key. However, you can use a proxy pattern: The control plane issues a session token. The agent calls the control plane's /exchange endpoint with the session token. The control plane returns a one-time API key that is valid for 15 minutes. The agent uses that key for its API calls. This is more secure because the key is never stored on the developer's machine. It exists only in memory for the duration of the session. The trade-off is that you need to implement a proxy for the model API calls, or the agent must support a custom auth flow. Some agents (like Claude Code) support custom API endpoints, which makes this feasible. Policy as Code We used YAML for policy definitions. But in 2026, the best practice is to express policy as code—specifically, as a set of functions that are evaluated against the request. This allows for complex logic like "allow this model only if the user is in the platform group and the repository is critical-infra ." Here's a TypeScript example using a policy-as-code approach: // policies/team-policy.ts import { PolicyContext , PolicyDecision } from "@controlplane/sdk" ; export default function evaluate ( ctx : PolicyContext ) : PolicyDecision { const { user , repo , agent , model , tools } = ctx ; // Deny if the user is not in the platform group if ( ! user . groups . includes ( "platform" ) ) { return { allowed : false , reason : "user not in platform group" } ; } // Deny if the repo is critical-infra and the agent is not codex if ( repo === "critical-infra" && agent . id !== "codex" ) { return { allowed : false , reason : "only codex allowed on critical-infra" } ; } // Allow only specific models if ( ! [ "anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet" , "openai/gpt-4o" ] . includes ( model ) ) { return { allowed : false , reason : "model not allowed" } ; } // Allow return { allowed : true , keyRef : `vault:secret/data/${agent.id}#api_key` , sessionTtl : 15 * 60 , } ; } This is much more flexible than YAML. You can unit test it, version it, and review it like any other code. The control plane loads these functions via a plugin system (e.g., WASM or a sandboxed JavaScript runtime). The Zero-Trust Agent Gateway In a zero-trust model, the control plane is the only component that can talk to the model providers. The agents themselves never have direct network access to the providers. Instead, the control plane acts as a gateway : The agent sends a request to the control plane's /proxy endpoint. The control plane validates the session, checks the policy, and forwards the request to the model provider with the API key. The provider's response is streamed back to the agent. This gives you complete visibility into every API call, the ability to rate-limit, and the ability to redact sensitive data in prompts. The downside is that you add latency and a single point of failure. In 2026, with the proliferation of local models, this is less of a concern because many requests can be served locally. Deep Dive: Cost Attribution and Metering The ledger plane is where the money is. In a BYOK world, the developer brings their own key, so you might think you don't need to track costs. But you do—because the whole point of a control plane is to provide a unified cost ledger across all providers, including local models. The Cost Model Every model provider has a different pricing structure. Some charge per token, some per request, some per second of compute. The ledger plane needs a normalized cost model. We'll define a simple schema: { "timestamp" : "2026-03-15T10:30:00Z" , "user_id" : "alice" , "agent_id" : "claude-code" , "model" : "anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet" , "tokens_in" : 12000 , "tokens_out" : 4500 , "cost_usd" : 0.0495 , "session_id" : "sess_123" , "metadata" : { "repo" : "acme/backend" , "branch" : "feature/foo" , "duration_ms" : 8500 } } The cost_usd is calculated by the runtime plane after the agent finishes, using the actual token counts returned by the provider. For local models, the cost is the opportunity cost of the compute time—you can estimate it based on the GPU hours consumed. The Metering Pipeline The ledger plane should not be a single Postgres table. In a high-throughput environment, you want an append-only log that is asynchronously aggregated. Here's a typical pipeline: The runtime plane writes a RunStarted event to a Kafka topic. The runtime plane writes a RunFinished event with the final token counts. A consumer joins the two events, calculates the cost, and writes to a time-series database (e.g., TimescaleDB or ClickHouse). A daily job aggregates the data into a summary table for dashboards. For our tutorial, we'll keep it simple with a JSONL file, but the pattern is the same. Chargeback and Budgets Once you have the ledger, you can implement budgets. The policy engine can query the ledger to check if a user or team has exceeded their monthly budget. If they have, the policy engine denies new runs. // In the policy engine's Authorize method: func ( e * PolicyEngine ) checkBudget ( ctx context . Context , userID string , agentID string ) ( bool , error ) { // Query the ledger for the current month's spend // If spend > budget, return false // This is a placeholder - in production, you'd use a SQL query. return true , nil } Anomaly Detection The ledger is also your security alarm. If a user suddenly starts requesting 10x their normal token usage, or if a user starts using a model they've never used before, the ledger plane can trigger an alert. This is the "canary in the coal mine" for compromised credentials. Deep Dive: Serverless Local Models The title mentions "Serverless Local Models." This is the most interesting and forward-looking part of the 2026 landscape. The idea is that you don't need to call an external API at all—you can run a model locally on your own hardware, but you want it to be serverless in the sense that it scales to zero and spins up on demand. The Local Model Runtime A serverless local model is a containerized inference server (e.g., vLLM, Ollama, or llama.cpp) that is started on demand. The control plane treats it like any other model provider, but instead of an API key, it needs a compute budget . agents : - id : "local-serverless" allowed_models : - "local/llama-3.1-8b" max_tokens_per_run : 50000 max_runs_per_day : 100 allowed_tools : - "read_file" - "write_file" - "bash" key_ref : "none" runtime : type : "serverless" image : "ghcr.io/acme/llama-server:latest" gpu : "a10g" max_idle_seconds : 60 min_instances : 0 max_instances : 4 When a request comes in for local/llama-3.1-8b , the runtime plane checks if an instance is already running. If not, it starts one (using a Kubernetes Deployment or a Knative Service). The agent then connects to the local endpoint (e.g., http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions ). After the run, the instance stays alive for max_idle_seconds and then scales to zero. The Cost of Local Models Local models have a different cost structure. The cost is not per token; it's per GPU-second. The ledger plane needs to account for this. We'll define a cost model that estimates the GPU cost based on the instance type and the duration of the run. func estimateLocalCost ( instanceType string , durationSeconds float64 ) float64 { // Example: $1.50 per hour for an A10G ratePerHour := map [ string ] float64 { "a10g" : 1.50 , "t4" : 0.80 , "l4" : 1.20 , } rate , ok := ratePerHour [ instanceType ] if ! ok { rate = 1.00 } return rate * ( durationSeconds / 3600.0 ) } The Hybrid Model The real power of a BYOK control plane is that it can choose between a local model and a cloud model based on policy. For example: If the request is for a simple code completion, use the local model (cheap, fast, private). If the request is for a complex refactoring, use Claude (expensive, but smarter). This is a routing decision that the policy engine makes. The developer doesn't choose; the control plane does. This is the ultimate form of lock-in prevention: you're not locked into any single provider because the control plane can switch providers transparently. Conclusion: The End of Lock-In We've covered a lot of ground. Let's recap the key architectural decisions: The control plane is the only component that holds keys. Agents never see them directly. Policy is code, not config. You can test it, version it, and review it. The ledger is the source of truth for cost and audit. Every decision is recorded. Local models are first-class citizens. They have the same policy and ledger treatment as cloud models. Routing is a policy decision. The control plane chooses the best model for the job, not the developer. The future of coding agents is not about which model wins. It's about which control plane wins. If you build a control plane that is provider-agnostic, policy-driven, and cost-aware, you will never be locked into a single agent again. Your developers will use whatever tool is best for the job, and your platform team will have a single place to enforce security, budget, and compliance. The agents will keep evolving. The models will keep commoditizing. But if you own the control plane, you control the future of your developer experience. This article is part of a series on infrastructure for AI development. The code examples are simplified for readability; production implementations should use proper error handling, observability, and security best practices.

title: Compute-in-Memory vs Von Neumann: Moving the Multiply to the Data
author: gxqwb
summary: Every AI accelerator is, underneath the marketing, a machine for moving numbers. The multiply-accumulate operations that make a transformer work are cheap; getting the weights to the multiplier is not. In a conventional chip, a weight travels from DRAM through several cache levels into a register, gets multiplied, and the partial sum travels back. Compute-in-memory (CIM) asks a blunt question: if the weight already sits in the memory array, why move it at all? A conventional accelerator can burn sixty to eighty percent of its energy on data movement, while a compute-in-memory array performs the multiply inside the memory cell itself — the savings come from deleting the bus, not from speeding up arithmetic. Part One: What is being compared The Von Neumann architecture separates storage from computation. A processor fetches instructions and operands from memory, computes, and writes results back. This separation is the reason a general-purpose computer can run any program, and it is also the reason a neural-network inference pass is memory-bound: for each weight you do one multiply, but that weight crosses a wire that is orders of magnitude more expensive than the multiply itself. Compute-in-memory collapses the two. In its dominant analog form, a crossbar of non-volatile memory cells — resistive RAM, flash, or phase-change — stores the weight as a conductance. Inputs are applied as voltages along the rows. Kirchhoff's law sums the currents at each column, and that sum is the dot product, computed by physics in a single step. No fetch, no register file, no separate ALU for that operation. The comparison is not "old versus new." It is a trade between flexibility and energy: a Von Neumann chip can compute anything but pays for every operand's journey; a CIM array does one operation beautifully and is locked to it. Part Two: The arithmetic Take a mainstream 7-nanometre accelerator running int8 inference. A DRAM access costs roughly 50 to 100 picojoules per byte, while a multiply-accumulate costs about 0.1 picojoules — a ratio of hundreds to one that is the entire case for moving the multiply into memory. That ratio — hundreds to one — is the entire case for CIM. A 7-billion-parameter model at int8 is 7 gigabytes of weights. Reading those weights once from DRAM costs on the order of 0.5 joules, while the arithmetic for one token is a few millijoules. The machine is a delivery service with a tiny factory attached. An analog CIM crossbar stores those weights in the array and applies inputs as voltage rows. The multiply and sum happen in the current flowing through the conductors, at maybe 1 to 10 femtojoules per operation — one to two orders of magnitude below the digital path. Published prototypes report energy efficiencies in the tens of tera-operations per watt for the in-array multiply, against single-digit tera-operations per watt for the best digital accelerators on the same process. The catch appears in the peripheries. Digital-to-analog and analog-to-digital converters sit at the edges of the crossbar, and they are power-hungry and area-hungry. A 128-by-128 array needs converters precise enough to preserve the signal; pushing their resolution up erases the energy win. The array also computes only matrix-vector products, so nonlinearities, normalization and attention softmax still run on conventional logic. Real chips end up hybrid, and the measured system-level gain is usually two to five times, not the hundred times the cell physics suggests. Part Three: Where the model breaks Analog computation is noisy in a way digital computation is not. Cell conductance drifts with temperature, with the number of program-erase cycles, and with the accumulated history of inputs. A weight written today is not exactly the weight read next month. On a 4-bit crossbar, device variation can push effective precision below what a quantized model tolerates, and accuracy drops unless the training procedure is taught to expect the noise. That is the deep asymmetry. A digital multiplier is deterministic: the same inputs always produce the same output, which is why software can be debugged. A CIM array is probabilistic hardware running a deterministic algorithm, so the system must either calibrate constantly — reading weights back and correcting — or train with noise injected so the network is robust to it. Both cost the very energy CIM was meant to save. There is also a programming-model tax. Digital accelerators run conventional frameworks with minor changes. CIM requires weights to be mapped onto physical cells, with aware placement to balance array utilization and tolerate defective cells. Toolchains exist but are immature, and a model that performs well in PyTorch may need substantial retraining and remapping before it runs correctly on the array. Part Four: The later cost The lifecycle differs in kind. A digital accelerator ages gracefully: a transistor slows slightly, timing margins absorb it, and the chip works. An analog CIM array ages as its memory cells age — resistive drift accumulates, and the accuracy curve degrades gradually over months rather than failing at a point. For a consumer device with a two-year life that may be invisible; for a datacentre accelerator expected to serve a decade, it is a maintenance problem nobody has fully priced. The failure modes also differ. Digital chips fail hard and are replaced. Analog arrays can fail soft — output accuracy quietly slips below spec while the chip still passes basic function checks — which is far more dangerous in a production inference pipeline. Detecting that requires on-chip reference circuits and periodic calibration, which again returns energy to the system. Manufacturing is the other tax. Resistive RAM and phase-change memory are not standard CMOS steps; adding them to a logic process raises cost and lowers yield, at least until the technology matures. Flash-based CIM avoids a novel process by reusing an established one, but flash is slow to program and wears out, which suits inference better than training. Part Five: Outside the team For the person using the product, the difference is battery and latency. A phone running an on-device assistant with a CIM accelerator can keep the model local instead of sending each query to a datacentre — better privacy, better offline behaviour, less network cost. The visible win is that the feature works on a plane and does not drain the battery by lunchtime. For the engineer, the choice decides what can ship. A digital NPU is boring to deploy and flexible when the model changes next quarter. A CIM block is efficient but opinionated: it rewards stable models, low precision and high batch reuse, and punishes rapid iteration. Teams whose model architecture changes monthly often find the flexibility of digital more valuable than the energy saving. For the environment, the arithmetic matters at scale. If inference grows to a significant share of global electricity use, a two-to-five-times efficiency gain on the dominant workload is material. But the gain must be measured at the system level, including converters, calibration and the digital logic that CIM cannot replace — not quoted from the crossbar alone. A fair comparison fixes the model, the precision target, the batch size and the acceptable accuracy loss, then measures joules per token at the wall socket. Quoting cell-level femtojoules against a system-level number is the most common way this comparison gets abused. Market sizing check If edge inference grows with the installed base of phones, cars and industrial sensors, and CIM captures even a quarter of the accelerator silicon in battery-powered devices, the addressable market for in-memory compute IP and chips is plausibly $8B to $20B a year by 2030. The swing factor is whether model architectures stabilise enough to justify hard-wiring them, and whether analog noise can be tamed without eating the energy budget. These figures are a synthesis of published market ranges and a stated model, not a forecast of any specific vendor. The comparison that matters The comparison that matters is between moving data and computing in place, priced at the wall socket. Von Neumann wins when the model changes often, precision requirements are high, and flexibility is worth more than efficiency. Compute-in-memory wins when the model is fixed, the precision target is modest, and energy per token is the binding constraint. The ranking assumes the workload is dominated by dense matrix multiplies. Shift toward attention-heavy or irregular computation and the fraction of work CIM can accelerate shrinks, taking its advantage with it. Compute-in-memory does not make arithmetic cheaper — it makes the data free by removing the journey, and that only pays when the arithmetic is regular enough to do inside the array. title: A Japan stock data API an agent can actually call
author: Ikkun
summary: The gap is not data, it is join keys Japan publishes more company data than most markets. EDINET has annual reports going back a decade, TDnet pushes earnings releases in near real time, JPX publishes listing files, and none of it costs money. If you are writing English documentation for an agent that needs Japanese financials, the problem is not supply. The problem is that every one of those sources identifies a company differently, and the mismatch shows up at the join, not at the download. I spent the last months building a data pipeline over these sources and then a tool layer on top of it. Here is what I measured on the way, and which route I ended up keeping. Route one: EDINET, official and free EDINET is the Financial Services Agency's disclosure system. It has a documented API, a subscription key, and document types for annual reports, semi-annual reports and extraordinary filings. For an agent that needs line-item detail, this is the only serious source, because the filings carry XBRL. Two things bite immediately. The first is the join key. EDINET's document list does not always tell you the ticker. On one day I pulled the list and got 5,741 documents, of which 3,694 came back without a securities code. That is 64 percent. Newly listed companies, foreign issuers and share-class filings are the usual suspects. If your loader keys on ticker only, two thirds of the day's filings silently fall out, and you will notice weeks later when a company you care about has a gap. The fallback is a two-step resolution: securities code first, then EDINET's own company code, then the filer name, normalised by folding full width characters and stripping the corporate form and punctuation. Name matching has to be fuzzy enough to survive "ＫＯＭＰＥＩＴＯ" against "株式会社コムペイト", and strict enough that two share classes of the same company do not collide. I chose to skip ambiguous matches rather than risk attributing a filing to the wrong entity. The second is that some filings have no numbers at all. Foreign companies come back with a flag that says no CSV is available, and the XBRL behind them contains no numeric facts, only converted HTML. Four of the companies in my universe are in that state. A pipeline that treats "no data" as "retry later" will retry forever. Route two: the JPX route J-Quants is the JPX-backed API, and it is where I would send someone who needs prices and valuation ratios with a clean contract. I did not benchmark it, and I am not going to quote its plan limits here: the site returned a 403 to my scripted requests, and publishing numbers I could not verify seemed worse than saying so. If the limits matter to your budget, read them on the site yourself. What I can say is what it does not carry: XBRL line items. If your agent needs to answer "what was in the segment note" or "what did the cash flow statement actually say", the JPX route is not the source for that question. The two are complementary, not substitutes. Route three: scrape the price pages The pragmatic route for daily prices is a library that scrapes a public quote page. I ran that for months. It works, with two traps I had to learn twice. First, the end date is exclusive. Pass today's date and today never lands, so your table looks one day stale forever. Second, in batch mode the most recent row often comes back with a null close, and if you write null rows you get holes that look like market holidays. Third, and this one hurt: never run the ingest during the session. A run at 09:27 wrote the intraday print as the close for 38 symbols, and because the freshness timestamp is derived from the newest row, the service reported "prices to today" while the values were wrong. The fix was to delete that day, republish, and move the job after the close. Freshness indicators are only as honest as the data they summarise. What actually costs the weeks None of the above is the hard part. The hard part is the vocabulary. Japanese filings use three accounting vocabularies: the domestic standard, IFRS, and US GAAP. The same line item can appear under three element names, and US GAAP inserts a token into the middle of the name rather than using a separate prefix. Build your map from IFRS samples alone and a whole block of companies comes back empty, including some of the largest. I found that out by diffing "companies with zero extracted revenue" against the listing file, which is the only reliable detector I have. The other trap is consolidation. A company's current year numbers can live only in a non-consolidated context. If you default to consolidated you get a row where the prior year is populated and the current year is null, which looks like a parsing bug but is a data shape. In my universe that affects 466 of roughly 3,700 companies. The detector cannot be the "consolidated / non-consolidated" column either, because it is frequently "other"; the reliable signal is the audit report element in the filing. What an agent needs on top Once the numbers are one schema, the remaining question is the interface. Agents do better with tools than with an SDK and a retry loop. So each endpoint in my service is also an MCP tool with typed arguments, and both surfaces run the same query layer with a parity test that compares the two outputs. Fourteen tools, fourteen endpoints, no second dialect to keep in sync. I measured the round trips from Tokyo against the hosted version. Five years of annual financials for Toyota is 10.5 KB and 0.56 seconds. A screen of 50 companies by ROE and PER is 27.6 KB and 0.21 seconds. Fifty disclosures is 15.6 KB and 0.31 seconds. Fifty XBRL line items is 7.8 KB and 0.28 seconds. Cold starts add to the first call after idle, and none of these numbers are promises. What this route does not give you Being clear about the edges is cheaper than a support ticket later. Prices start in 2023 and are not split adjusted in this release. There is no real time feed and no order book. Forecast data only exists for companies that filed an earnings release while the source still keeps it, and that source keeps roughly one month, so guidance coverage is narrower than financial statement coverage by construction. Nothing here is investment advice, and it is not a licensed vendor for regulated use. Where this landed I put the result behind a free key: an MCP server and REST API over EDINET, TDnet and JPX, with five years of financials, XBRL line items, disclosures, screening and rankings. One hundred calls a month, no card. The product page and the key form are at discli , and the API contract is in the EDINET API v2 notes if you want to build the ingest yourself instead. If you have wired Japanese filings into an agent, which part cost you the most: the join key, the vocabulary, or the freshness lie? Originally published at agentjournal.dev .

title: Pick the Model Per Task, Not Per Project: My Aider Cost-Control Rules
author: nexus ai
summary: Aider is free. The model isn't. Every message you send carries the repo map, your added files, and the chat history — so cost control in Aider is mostly context control. These are the rules that keep my bill boring. Pick by role, not by brand Aider has three model roles: the main editor, a weak model (commit messages, summaries), and — in architect mode — an architect plus an editor. My simplified matrix: Learning / small projects: a mid-tier frontier model as main, a mini/Haiku-class model as weak. Mid-tier edits reliably at a fraction of flagship prices. Hard, multi-file features: flagship model, or architect mode — flagship architect planning, mid-tier editor executing. Planning tokens are cheaper than wrong-edit tokens. Bulk mechanical edits (renames, format migrations): a low-cost model is fine. Review the diffs closely. Private / offline code: a local model via Ollama. $0 marginal cost; slower and weaker — know the trade you're making. Huge repo, mostly questions: a large-context model in /ask mode. Questions need context room, not editing reliability. The five habits that actually move the bill Set a weak model. Commit messages and history summaries run constantly. On a flagship main model, they quietly tax every single edit. One config line removes that tax. Curate context like it's metered — because it is. /add only what will be edited, /read-only for reference, /drop when done. /tokens shows what you're carrying. A file left in chat "just in case" is paid for on every message. Size the repo map. On large repos, a smaller map-tokens setting trims what Aider sends each turn. Turn on prompt caching once your workflow is stable ( --cache-prompts , notably effective with Claude models). It cuts the cost of re-sent context in long sessions. Start fresh between tasks. History accumulates tokens. /clear or a new session per task. When cheap is expensive Cheap models fail predictably: mangled edit formats, ignored instructions, loops that burn 10 turns doing what a strong model does in one. My rule: if a session needs more than ~3 corrective prompts on the same edit, I switch the main model up a tier mid-session ( /model ). My time is the scarcest token in the system. And one honesty note: Aider's in-session cost figures are estimates . Your provider's usage dashboard is the bill of record — check it, and check current prices before a long session, because they change too often to print.
